findings.issue_text: [BUG] LoginValues gains a backupCode field but the zod formSchema driving zodResolver is not updated in this diff, so the resolver strips the unregistered key and credentials.backupCode is never sent. A user who clicks 'Lost access' and submits a backup code gets a form payload with no backupCode; next-auth's authorize() falls through to the TOTP branch with an empty totpCode and returns SecondFactorRequired, so backup-code login can never succeed and the UI re-shows the TOTP prompt with no explanation.

[BUG] The download button inside the Form has no type="button" and no e.preventDefault(), so clicking it submits the form. Clicking 'Download' on the backup-codes step fires handleSubmit(handleEnable) with an empty totpCode, hitting the enable endpoint a second time (re-running setup/enable logic) instead of just downloading the file; the close/copy buttons each call e.preventDefault() so only the download button triggers this.

[ADVISORY] A <Button> (renders <button>) is nested inside an <a download> element, which is invalid HTML (interactive element inside an anchor). Browsers/assistive tech get contradictory interactive semantics; the button's own click handling can race with the anchor navigation, and any future refactor to the Button component (e.g. adding onClick) silently breaks the download path. Maintainers bitten on the next change to this footer.

[ADVISORY] The default export in BackupCode.tsx is still declared as `function TwoFactor`, duplicating the name of the existing component in TwoFactor.tsx. Stack traces, React DevTools, and import-site debugging all show 'TwoFactor' for the backup-code component; the next person diffing or grepping the 2FA flow conflates the two components and edits the wrong file.

[ADVISORY] Backup-code consumption (read, null-out, re-encrypt, update) is not atomic — the indexOf/decrypt and the prisma.user.update are separate operations with no transaction or conditional update. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code both pass indexOf and both succeed, violating the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' guarantee shown to the user in backup_code_instructions.

[ADVISORY] Once all ten codes are consumed, user.backupCodes remains the JSON string "[null,null,...]" which is truthy, so the MissingBackupCodes branch is unreachable for exhausted users. A user who has burned every code and lost their authenticator gets 'Backup Code is incorrect.' instead of the intended 'No backup codes found', and the DisableTwoFactorModal shows the same misleading message — a support dead-end for exactly the locked-out user the feature exists for.

[ADVISORY] The setup endpoint returns the plaintext backupCodes array in the JSON response while also persisting it encrypted. The codes appear unencrypted in any response logging, proxy capture, or browser cache of the setup call; users who enable 2FA and later abandon the flow (never reaching DisplayBackupCodes) have live backup codes they never saw, silently weakening the single-use contract.

[ADVISORY] The missing-CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY check throws raw Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) instead of returning a JSON error response like every other branch in the handler. An operator with a misconfigured env hits a thrown error that surfaces as an unhandled 500 stack trace rather than the {error: 'internal-server-error'} JSON contract the DisableTwoFactorModal error handling expects, so the client shows the generic fallback with no diagnostics.

[BUG] The diff's own TODO comment admits there is no test for logging in with a backup code or disabling 2FA with a backup code, and no test in the diff exercises the next-auth authorize backup-code branch, the backup-code consumption logic, or the disable endpoint's backup-code branch. The core security behavior of this feature (backup code verification, single-use consumption via backupCodes[index] = null, and clearing codes on disable) ships with zero regression coverage; a future refactor of symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse in next-auth-options.ts or disable.ts breaks backup-code login silently and no CI test fails. The e2e test present in the diff only covers the DisplayBackupCodes UI buttons (download filename, copy toast, close).

[BUG] There is no attempt limit or rate limiting on backup-code verification in the authorize callback, and the two-factor disable endpoint's backup-code branch likewise has no throttling. An attacker with a stolen password can brute-force backup codes through the login form without limit; unlike the TOTP path (6 digits, also unthrottled), this diff adds a brand-new verification surface (10 hex chars) but reuses no rate limiter even though checkRateLimitAndThrowError is imported and used elsewhere in this file's flow. Users with weak backup codes face unbounded guessing attempts.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code input does no case normalization or whitespace trimming, while verification does a strict indexOf on the lower-hex code after only stripping dashes. A user who types the code in uppercase (the display shows it in hex; hex is commonly typed uppercase) or with a leading/trailing space fails verification with "Backup code is incorrect" even though they entered the correct code. Rebuttal: 'users copy-paste' — but the placeholder XXXXX-XXXXX invites manual entry and the login page is the one path users hit under stress; the copy path is fine, the manual path is broken.

[ADVISORY] setup.ts persists encrypted backup codes unconditionally (and regenerates them on every setup call) with no CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY presence check, unlike the verify paths which guard it. If the env var is missing, symmetricEncrypt runs with an undefined key; depending on crypto.ts it either throws a 500 at setup or stores backupCodes encrypted under an undefined/garbage key, after which every later backup-code login throws InternalServerError. Additionally, a user who starts setup (generating codes shown in the modal) but abandons the flow before enabling TOTP retains stale unshown codes in the DB that a later enable never regenerates if setup isn't re-called — the user may believe their displayed codes are current when the DB holds a different set from the most recent abandoned setup call.

[ADVISORY] The backupCodesUrl object URL is only revoked when a new setup response arrives; it is never revoked in resetState or on dialog close/unmount. Each open/setup cycle of the enable modal leaks a Blob object URL for the lifetime of the SPA page; a user repeatedly toggling 2FA in a long-lived settings session accumulates leaked blobs. Minor memory leak, staff-worthy but not blocking.

[ADVISORY] The new component's default export is declared as `function TwoFactor` while living in BackupCode.tsx, a copy-paste of the sibling file's signature. The next engineer grepping for the BackupCode component or reading a React DevTools tree sees two components named TwoFactor; stack traces and debugging of the login backup-code path are misleading, and a future rename of one will miss the other because they share a name.

[ADVISORY] Toggling "Lost access" clears totpCode but the login zod formSchema (LoginValues gains backupCode but the resolver schema is not shown updated in this diff) and the Back button render unconditionally even on the ExternalTotpFooter path context, leaving the lost-access toggle only in TwoFactorFooter while the totpEmail external footer offers no backup-code escape. A user who arrived via totpEmail (external verification flow) and has lost their authenticator has no backup-code path at all — the lost_access button exists only in the standard TwoFactorFooter, so the feature silently does not cover the totpEmail login variant.

[BUG] Backup codes are generated and persisted at the setup step, before 2FA is actually enabled, so calling setup without completing enable leaves orphaned codes in the DB and a second setup call silently regenerates them with no trace in the UI. A user who opens the enable dialog (setup runs), abandons it, later re-enables 2FA, and loses their authenticator will try backup codes from the only place they were ever shown (or not shown at all, since codes are only displayed after the enable step of the latest setup run); any codes from an earlier setup run are silently invalidated, so a user who saved codes from one attempt is locked out by a later attempt.

[BUG] backupCodes are written via symmetricEncrypt(process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) at setup time with no CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY guard in this handler, unlike disable.ts which explicitly checks it before decrypting. On a deployment missing the encryption key, setup crashes with an unhandled symmetricEncrypt failure (undefined key) instead of a 400/500 with a stable ErrorCode, and the user's twoFactorSecret update and the whole enable flow fails opaquely.

[BUG] The used backup code is invalidated by `backupCodes[index] = null` followed by a separate prisma.user.update, with no transaction and no re-check, and the comparison uses indexOf (non-constant-time) on a 10-char hex code. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code is consumed twice — breaking the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' invariant the UI copy (backup_code_instructions) explicitly promises; the indexOf comparison also leaks a timing side channel relative to the position of the code in the array.

[BUG] The backup-code login path throws new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes / IncorrectBackupCode) and performs a DB write inside authorize() before the session/JWT is created, so a successful write followed by a later authorize failure (or a retry) leaves the code already burned. If anything after the prisma.user.update in authorize fails (session callback, JWT, network retry of the credentials signin), the user's backup code is consumed without them being logged in; combined with the login page's generic fallback this produces unexplained code exhaustion for users on flaky connections.

[ADVISORY] The missing_backup_codes error copy instructs 'Please generate them in your settings', but this diff contains no settings surface to generate or regenerate backup codes — regeneration only happens implicitly by re-running 2FA setup. Users who exhaust their 10 codes hit a dead-end message pointing at functionality that does not exist; the only recovery is fully disabling and re-enabling 2FA, which the message does not describe.

[ADVISORY] Adding tabIndex={-1} to the PasswordField visibility toggle button is unrelated to 2FA backup codes and is an untraceable scope expansion to a shared UI package component. Keyboard users of every PasswordField in the app can no longer Tab to the show/hide password toggle; the change ships inside a 2FA PR with no requirement or test justifying it, so it escapes review by reviewers scoped to auth behavior.

[ADVISORY] The component in BackupCode.tsx is declared as `export default function TwoFactor`, shadowing the real TwoFactor component name. Importers and stack traces/debuggers will label backup-code UI as 'TwoFactor'; a future refactor grepping for TwoFactor will match this file and mis-edit it, degrading change-safety of the auth component pair.

[ADVISORY] The new backupCodesUrl object URL is created in handleSetup and only revoked when a new one replaces it; onEnable via the DisplayBackupCodes close path and the dialog's own onOpenChange close both tear down the modal without revoking the final object URL, and backupCodes state also survives unmount paths that bypass resetState. Each abandoned enable flow leaks a Blob URL in the page until navigation, and a reopened modal briefly retains stale codes/state when closed via DialogContent's X (which calls onCancel + resetState but not the onEnable path, so the settings switch also never reflects the now-enabled 2FA server state).

[ADVISORY] The PR ships its headline backup-code login/disable behaviors with only download/copy/close UI tests; there is no test that a backup code actually logs a user in, that it is single-use, or that it disables 2FA — the TODO comment in the diff acknowledges this gap. The entire server-side consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts (null-ing used codes, re-encrypting) and the disable.ts backup-code branch ship with zero coverage, so the single-use invariant regressing would not fail any test.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated only in setup.ts, which is only reachable before 2FA is enabled, so every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy has backupCodes = null and no path to ever obtain codes. Existing 2FA users who lose their authenticator hit the new 'missing_backup_codes' dead end ('Please generate them in your settings') — but no settings UI or API regenerates codes for an already-enabled account; their only recovery is the very TOTP they lost. The error message advertises a flow that does not exist.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: the code is checked with indexOf, then nulled and the whole list re-encrypted in a separate update with no transaction or version guard. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, and the second write clobbers the first's null — a single-use code is accepted twice (single-use invariant broken), and one of the two updates is silently lost.

[BUG] backupCode was added to LoginValues but the zod formSchema driving zodResolver was not updated, so the resolver strips the field on submit and credentials.backupCode is always undefined. The 'lost access' backup-code login path can never actually authenticate: the server sees no backupCode, falls into the TOTP branch, and returns SecondFactorRequired — the user is stuck in a loop with the error 'Backup code is incorrect' never reachable through this form.

[ADVISORY] The comparison `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` matches the raw stored lowercase-hex string against untrimmed, case-sensitive user input. A user who types an uppercase backup code (or pastes with a trailing space/newline) is told the code is incorrect even though it is valid; the write side stores lowercase hex with no normalization on the read side — a format-drift between what the UI shows and what the lookup expects.

[ADVISORY] BackupCode.tsx declares `export default function TwoFactor`, shadowing the name of the real TwoFactor component that both files import alongside each other (login.tsx imports both BackupCode and TwoFactor). The next editor grepping for TwoFactor or copy-pasting an import lands on the wrong component; the confusable-pair binding also makes future diffs easy to mis-review (e.g. swapping the BackupCode/TwoFactor render branches in login.tsx).

[BUG] The missing-backup-codes error message tells users to "generate them in your settings", but this diff ships no regeneration path — backup codes are created only inside the enable-2FA setup flow (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:60) and can never be re-displayed or regenerated afterward. A user who has consumed some/all backup codes (each login use nulls one out in next-auth-options.ts:144-152) and then visits settings as instructed finds no "generate backup codes" control; the promised recovery path does not exist, so the shipped UX contradicts the lost-access recovery intent of the feature.

[BUG] The setup endpoint persists a fresh set of backup codes to the user row before 2FA is ever enabled, so any user who reaches the DisplayBackupCodes step and then cancels (or fails TOTP verification and retries setup) silently invalidates the codes they already copied/downloaded. A user who downloads cal-backup-codes.txt from a first enable attempt, abandons it at the TOTP step, and later completes a second attempt ends up with a saved file of dead codes; the next time they use the lost-access flow with those codes they get IncorrectBackupCode and are locked out — exactly the recovery scenario the feature exists to serve.

[BUG] setup.ts calls symmetricEncrypt(..., process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) without the missing-key guard that disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts both have, so when CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset the setup endpoint crashes. User hits 500 InternalServerError on the 2FA setup step instead of a graceful error; in deployments where the key is missing/unset the whole enable-2FA flow is broken with an unhandled exception rather than a controlled error.

[BUG] The backup-code single-use enforcement is a non-atomic read-then-write: the decrypted list is searched with indexOf and the code is nulled in a separate prisma.user.update, so two concurrent authorize() calls using the same backup code both find index !== -1 and both succeed before either write lands. A backup code advertised as usable 'exactly once' can be replayed to log in twice (or once for login and once for the disable endpoint, which also only checks indexOf), breaking the single-use invariant the UI text promises; an attacker who phished a code gets multiple sessions.

[ADVISORY] Backup-code verification has no attempt counter or lockout specific to it and compares a 40-bit hex (crypto.randomBytes(5)) code with plain indexOf, so nothing in this diff bounds guessing of the 10 valid codes beyond whatever generic rate limiter guards the credentials endpoint. An attacker with a stolen password can grind backup-code guesses at the rate limit (10 targets across ~2^40 keyspace materially improves per-request success odds vs a single code); users relying on a backup code after losing their authenticator get an account takeover if a lockout tier doesn't already cover it.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted on the setup call — which only requires the account password — before 2FA is actually enabled, and they survive if the user abandons the flow at the QR step. A user who starts but never completes enabling 2FA has 10 live one-factor-equal credentials stored (returning MissingBackupCodes confusion later, and if any future code path checks backupCodes without checking twoFactorEnabled they become a password-bypass); also each abandoned re-setup silently invalidates previously downloaded codes, so a user with saved codes printed from an earlier attempt is locked out via that path.

[ADVISORY] The new backup-code login flow (lost_access toggle, BackupCode input, and the corresponding next-auth-options.ts authorize backupCode branch at packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts lines 131-157) is exercised by no test in this diff — the only spec touched is apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts, and its own newly-added comment at line 12 says '// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. A regression in backup-code login (wrong error mapping, the single-use consumption path backupCodes[index] = null, or the dash-stripping in replaceAll("-", "")) ships silently; users locked out of their authenticator are permanently locked out, which is the exact scenario backup codes exist to prevent.

[ADVISORY] The new backup-code branch in the disable endpoint (MissingBackupCodes, IncorrectBackupCode, decrypt+indexOf matching, and the backupCodes: null wipe at line 107) has zero test coverage — no spec file in the diff references disable or backupCode, and the diff's own TODO at login.2fa.e2e.ts line 12 admits 'disabling 2fa with backup' is untested. The disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts implementations duplicate the same match/dash-strip logic but diverge (login deletes the used code; disable wipes all codes only on success) — this drift is invisible to the suite, so a fix applied to one copy will not be validated against the other and users who disable via backup code could have stale/consumed codes left behind.

[ADVISORY] The new e2e backup-codes steps assert only side-channel signals: download checks download.suggestedFilename() (not file content) and copy checks the toast appears (not clipboard content) — both gaps are explicitly acknowledged by the newly added '// TODO: check file content' and '// TODO: check clipboard content' comments, so the test passes even if the download/copy payload is empty or contains unformatted codes. formatBackupCode (the 5-5 hyphen split the server-side matcher's replaceAll("-","") depends on) is never validated end-to-end; a regression that copies raw 10-char codes or an empty string still yields a green build, and users who saved the file get codes the login matcher will accept only by luck of dash handling.

[ADVISORY] The diff itself documents a false-confidence assertion it leaves in place: the newly added comment '// FIXME: this passes even when switch is not checked' on the expect(...isChecked()).toBeTruthy() assertion at the 2FA switch — the test asserts 2FA is enabled using an assertion the author observed passing in the unchecked state. The only assertion in the whole suite that the 2FA enable flow actually persisted twoFactorEnabled can pass on failure, so this diff's core deliverable (successful 2FA enable producing backup codes) has no trustworthy end-state check; the file-content TODO above compounds it.

[ADVISORY] Existing 2FA-enabled users have backupCodes NULL forever because the migration adds a nullable column with no backfill and no regeneration path for accounts that already have twoFactorEnabled=true. Any user who enabled 2FA before this deploy hits the 'lost access' login flow, receives MissingBackupCodes ('No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.'), and cannot generate codes without first disabling 2FA — which itself requires a TOTP code they no longer have — locking them out exactly in the scenario backup codes exist to rescue.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted to the user row at the password-confirmation step, before 2FA is enabled, and every invocation of setup silently overwrites previously stored codes. A user who confirms their password, downloads the displayed codes, then restarts the enable flow (e.g. cancels at the TOTP step and reopens the modal) gets a fresh setup call that invalidates the already-downloaded codes without any indication; they later authenticate with a code from the stale download and receive IncorrectBackupCode despite never misbehaving.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are shown exactly once in the DisplayBackupCodes step and no endpoint or UI exists to re-display or regenerate them while 2FA stays enabled. A user who closes the dialog without copying/downloading permanently loses access to their codes (setup.ts cannot be re-run while twoFactorEnabled=true), so losing the authenticator later means the only remaining path is account-level recovery instead of a backup code.

[BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) runs with no try/catch, so a corrupt or undecryptable backupCodes value throws an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of the 4xx the endpoint's contract promises. A user whose backupCodes column holds invalid ciphertext (or CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY rotated) hits a raw 500 on every disable attempt with no actionable error, while every other failure path on this endpoint returns a 400 with an ErrorCode.

[BUG] The verified backup code is nulled and persisted to the DB before the remainder of authorize() runs, so any later failure in authorize burns the code without granting a login. A user who submits a valid backup code but then trips a subsequent failure in authorize (e.g., an org/SSO check throwing) permanently loses that one-time code and receives only a generic login error — the code is consumed with no way to recover it, and there is no log of the consumption.

[BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) is unguarded, so decrypt/parse failure throws mid-authorize and produces an internal next-auth error rather than the MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode 4xx-shaped errors the rest of the branch uses. Users with corrupt stored backup codes get a raw internal error on every login attempt, and the failure mode is indistinguishable from a server outage.

[BUG] Closing the dialog via ESC or the Dialog X at the DisplayBackupCodes step (onOpenChange path) skips resetState and onEnable, so the backup codes are persisted server-side but never shown again and no regeneration path exists. A user who starts typing/copying their codes and accidentally hits ESC loses all 10 backup codes permanently: the codes were stored at setup/enable time, there is no API to re-display or regenerate them (only full disable + re-enable, which itself now requires a working second factor), and the parent UI never learns 2FA was enabled. Silent data loss on a user-facing flow.

[ADVISORY] navigator.clipboard.writeText is fire-and-forget: the success toast shows immediately without awaiting the promise, so a rejected write (insecure context, permission denied) is silently swallowed while the UI reports success. Users on non-HTTPS deployments or with clipboard permission revoked are told 'Backup codes copied!' when nothing was copied — and for one-time-use codes this is data loss, since the codes can never be re-displayed.

[ADVISORY] backupCodesUrl object URL is revoked only when a new one is generated and never on resetState/unmount, leaking one Blob-backed URL per setup run. Users who open the enable-2FA flow repeatedly accumulate leaked object URLs/Blobs for the lifetime of the page; minor but unbounded across repeated toggling in one session.

[ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component's function is named TwoFactor while the actual TwoFactor component also exists and is imported elsewhere, so stack traces, React DevTools, and error boundaries all mislabel this component as the TOTP input. Anyone debugging a form error in the backup-code flow is misdirected to the wrong component; the copy-paste origin also means future edits to one are likely to be applied to the wrong file.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted at setup time (before the user ever completes the TOTP verification step), so each aborted-and-restarted setup silently discards previously issued codes and a user who saw codes from an earlier setup attempt (e.g., in a parallel tab) has those codes invalidated without any indication. Two concurrent setup sessions (two tabs, or setup then re-setup before enabling) overwrite each other's backup codes; the earlier-shown codes silently fail at login with IncorrectBackupCode and the user has no way to know which set is current.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The setup endpoint persists a fresh set of backup codes to the user row before 2FA is ever enabled, so any user who reaches the DisplayBackupCodes step and then cancels (or fails TOTP verification and retries setup) silently invalidates the codes they already copied/downloaded. A user who downloads cal-backup-codes.txt from a first enable attempt, abandons it at the TOTP step, and later completes a second attempt ends up with a saved file of dead codes; the next time they use the lost-access flow with those codes they get IncorrectBackupCode and are locked out — exactly the recovery scenario the feature exists to serve.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` generating and persisting `backupCodes` immediately (`prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: ..., twoFactorEnabled: false, twoFactorSecret: ... } })`) before 2FA is actually enabled. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] setup.ts calls symmetricEncrypt(..., process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) without the missing-key guard that disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts both have, so when CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset the setup endpoint crashes. adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, the PR adds `backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` and still calls `symmetricEncrypt(..., process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` without any check that `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The backup-code single-use enforcement is a non-atomic read-then-write: the decrypted list is searched with indexOf and the code is nulled in a separate prisma.user.update, so two concurrent authorize() calls using the same backup code both find index !== -1 and both succeed before either write lands. A backup code advertised as usable 'exactly once' can be replayed to log in twice (or once for login and once for the disable endpoint, which also only checks indexOf), breaking the single-use invariant the UI text promises; an attacker who phished a code gets multiple sessions.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup-code validation is implemented as a non-atomic read/modify/write: decrypt `user.backupCodes`, `indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`, then later `prisma.user.update` sets `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts. Two concurrent `authorize()` calls can both observe the same unused code (index != -1) before either update commits, allowing the same backup code to be accepted more than once, violating the "exactly once" promise. Additionally, `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` similarly checks `indexOf` on decrypted codes without consuming a specific code (it only clears all codes at the end when disabling), so the validation itself is also non-atomic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup-code verification has no attempt counter or lockout specific to it and compares a 40-bit hex (crypto.randomBytes(5)) code with plain indexOf, so nothing in this diff bounds guessing of the 10 valid codes beyond whatever generic rate limiter guards the credentials endpoint. An attacker with a stolen password can grind backup-code guesses at the rate limit (10 targets across ~2^40 keyspace materially improves per-request success odds vs a single code); users relying on a backup code after losing their authenticator get an account takeover if a lockout tier doesn't already cover it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces backup-code auth paths in both the credentials authorize flow (`next-auth-options.ts`: checks `credentials.backupCode` and uses `indexOf` against decrypted codes) and the 2FA disable API (`pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`: checks `req.body.backupCode` similarly). In neither place does the diff add any per-user attempt counter, lockout, or throttling specific to backup-code verification; the code simply checks membership and returns an error. Because there are 10 valid codes (generated in `totp/setup.ts` via `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`) a guess has higher success probability than a single secret, so online guessing risk is increased unless other (not-shown) rate limits cover it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted on the setup call — which only requires the account password — before 2FA is actually enabled, and they survive if the user abandons the flow at the QR step. A user who starts but never completes enabling 2FA has 10 live one-factor-equal credentials stored (returning MissingBackupCodes confusion later, and if any future code path checks backupCodes without checking twoFactorEnabled they become a password-bypass); also each abandoned re-setup silently invalidates previously downloaded codes, so a user with saved codes printed from an earlier attempt is locked out via that path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show backup codes are generated and persisted in the setup endpoint before 2FA is enabled (`setup.ts` stores `backupCodes` while setting `twoFactorEnabled: false`). However, the finding’s core claim that this creates “10 live one-factor-equal credentials” / “password-bypass” is not supported by the diff: both login and disable paths only accept backup codes when `user.twoFactorEnabled` is true (`next-auth-options.ts`: `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`, and `disable.ts`: `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && req.body.backupCode)`). Also, the UI only displays/copies/downloads backup codes after enabling succeeds (`EnableTwoFactorModal` moves to `DisplayBackupCodes` only after `/enable` returns 200), so abandoning at the QR step doesn’t produce “previously downloaded codes” from that abandoned attempt. The rest (future code paths, confusion/lockout) is speculative beyond what the diff shows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Existing 2FA-enabled users have backupCodes NULL forever because the migration adds a nullable column with no backfill and no regeneration path for accounts that already have twoFactorEnabled=true. Any user who enabled 2FA before this deploy hits the 'lost access' login flow, receives MissingBackupCodes ('No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.'), and cannot generate codes without first disabling 2FA — which itself requires a TOTP code they no longer have — locking them out exactly in the scenario backup codes exist to rescue.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a nullable `backupCodes` column (migration + schema) but only ever populates it during the new TOTP setup endpoint (`/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts` generates and stores encrypted `backupCodes`). There is no path in the diff that generates backup codes for users who already have `twoFactorEnabled=true` prior to this deploy. As a result, in the new “lost access” flow, both login (`next-auth-options.ts`: `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode) { if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes }`) and disable-2FA (`totp/disable.ts`: `if (!user.backupCodes) return MissingBackupCodes`) will reject those users with `MissingBackupCodes`. The UI message suggests generating codes in settings, but a user who lost their TOTP cannot log in to reach settings, so the new recovery feature fails for the exact legacy cohort it should help.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted to the user row at the password-confirmation step, before 2FA is enabled, and every invocation of setup silently overwrites previously stored codes. A user who confirms their password, downloads the displayed codes, then restarts the enable flow (e.g. cancels at the TOTP step and reopens the modal) gets a fresh setup call that invalidates the already-downloaded codes without any indication; they later authenticate with a code from the stale download and receive IncorrectBackupCode despite never misbehaving.

adjudication.rationale: While `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` does generate and persist `backupCodes` immediately (and will overwrite them on each setup call), the finding’s user story isn’t supported by the diff: in `EnableTwoFactorModal`, backup codes are only displayed/downloadable in `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and the code transitions to that step only after the enable call succeeds (`handleEnable`: `if (response.status === 200) { setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes); }`). A user cannot “download the displayed codes” and then “cancel at the TOTP step” because the UI doesn’t show download/copy controls until after TOTP enable has already completed. The harmful consequence (ending up with a stale downloaded code without indication) is therefore not verifiable from the shown flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are shown exactly once in the DisplayBackupCodes step and no endpoint or UI exists to re-display or regenerate them while 2FA stays enabled. A user who closes the dialog without copying/downloading permanently loses access to their codes (setup.ts cannot be re-run while twoFactorEnabled=true), so losing the authenticator later means the only remaining path is account-level recovery instead of a backup code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds generation/storage of `backupCodes` in `setup.ts` and only surfaces them in the new `EnableTwoFactorModal` step `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes` (rendered via `backupCodes.map(...)` plus copy/download). There is no other UI or API shown here to re-display/regenerate backup codes once the user closes that dialog, so from the user’s perspective they effectively lose access to the codes if they don’t copy/download them at that moment. However, the claim that `setup.ts` “cannot be re-run while twoFactorEnabled=true” is not verifiable from this diff (the enable endpoint/guards aren’t shown), so the finding is more of a product/flow completeness concern than a strict defect provable from the patch alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) runs with no try/catch, so a corrupt or undecryptable backupCodes value throws an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of the 4xx the endpoint's contract promises. A user whose backupCodes column holds invalid ciphertext (or CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY rotated) hits a raw 500 on every disable attempt with no actionable error, while every other failure path on this endpoint returns a 400 with an ErrorCode.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new backup-code path does `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY));` with no error handling. If `symmetricDecrypt` throws (e.g., wrong/rotated `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, corrupted ciphertext) or the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON, the handler will throw and Next.js will return a 500 rather than the endpoint’s established pattern of returning `400` with an `ErrorCode` for user-facing failures. This failure mode is introduced by the diff (backupCodes support).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The verified backup code is nulled and persisted to the DB before the remainder of authorize() runs, so any later failure in authorize burns the code without granting a login. A user who submits a valid backup code but then trips a subsequent failure in authorize (e.g., an org/SSO check throwing) permanently loses that one-time code and receives only a generic login error — the code is consumed with no way to recover it, and there is no log of the consumption.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` inside `authorize()`, when `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` matches, the code immediately mutates and persists backup codes (`backupCodes[index] = null; await prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...) }})`) before the rest of `authorize()` completes. The diff does not show any transaction/rollback or deferring this update until after all other checks succeed, so any later `throw`/failure in `authorize()` would reject the login while still consuming the one-time backup code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) is unguarded, so decrypt/parse failure throws mid-authorize and produces an internal next-auth error rather than the MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode 4xx-shaped errors the rest of the branch uses. Users with corrupt stored backup codes get a raw internal error on every login attempt, and the failure mode is indistinguishable from a server outage.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, the backup-code branch does `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY));` with no try/catch. If decryption fails (wrong key/garbled ciphertext) or the decrypted string is not valid JSON, `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` will throw a non-`ErrorCode` error, causing next-auth to surface a generic internal error instead of the intended `MissingBackupCodes`/`IncorrectBackupCode` errors used elsewhere in that branch. The diff shows no guarding or conversion of those failures into a known error code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Closing the dialog via ESC or the Dialog X at the DisplayBackupCodes step (onOpenChange path) skips resetState and onEnable, so the backup codes are persisted server-side but never shown again and no regeneration path exists. A user who starts typing/copying their codes and accidentally hits ESC loses all 10 backup codes permanently: the codes were stored at setup/enable time, there is no API to re-display or regenerate them (only full disable + re-enable, which itself now requires a working second factor), and the parent UI never learns 2FA was enabled. Silent data loss on a user-facing flow.

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal, a successful enable sets `step` to `DisplayBackupCodes` and intentionally does *not* call `onEnable()` (it only calls `onEnable()` from the explicit “close” button handler in that step). However, the Dialog can also be closed via `onOpenChange` (ESC / X), and this component does not wrap/intercept `onOpenChange` to call `resetState()` and/or `onEnable()` when `step === DisplayBackupCodes`. Therefore, closing the dialog through that path can leave the parent unaware 2FA was enabled while backup codes were already generated/stored during setup (`/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` updates `backupCodes`) and there is no UI/API in this diff to re-display them. This matches the finding’s core behavior (skipped reset/onEnable via onOpenChange and loss of one-time display of codes).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] navigator.clipboard.writeText is fire-and-forget: the success toast shows immediately without awaiting the promise, so a rejected write (insecure context, permission denied) is silently swallowed while the UI reports success. Users on non-HTTPS deployments or with clipboard permission revoked are told 'Backup codes copied!' when nothing was copied — and for one-time-use codes this is data loss, since the codes can never be re-displayed.

adjudication.rationale: In `EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx`, the copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` and immediately executes `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` without `await`/`.then`/`.catch` (see the `data-testid="backup-codes-copy"` button). If `writeText` rejects (e.g., insecure context, permissions), the UI will still report success and the rejection is unhandled, so the finding is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] backupCodesUrl object URL is revoked only when a new one is generated and never on resetState/unmount, leaking one Blob-backed URL per setup run. Users who open the enable-2FA flow repeatedly accumulate leaked object URLs/Blobs for the lifetime of the page; minor but unbounded across repeated toggling in one session.

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal, a Blob-backed object URL is created on successful setup (`setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))`) and the previous URL is only revoked when generating a new one (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). The `resetState()` used on cancel/close does not revoke `backupCodesUrl`, nor is there an unmount cleanup via `useEffect`, so repeated runs of the flow can accumulate unreclaimed object URLs/Blobs for the lifetime of the page.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component's function is named TwoFactor while the actual TwoFactor component also exists and is imported elsewhere, so stack traces, React DevTools, and error boundaries all mislabel this component as the TOTP input. Anyone debugging a form error in the backup-code flow is misdirected to the wrong component; the copy-paste origin also means future edits to one are likely to be applied to the wrong file.

React DevTools and many stack traces typically use the function name as the component name, so this will show up as `TwoFactor`, which can mislead debugging and error attribution. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted at setup time (before the user ever completes the TOTP verification step), so each aborted-and-restarted setup silently discards previously issued codes and a user who saw codes from an earlier setup attempt (e.g., in a parallel tab) has those codes invalidated without any indication. Two concurrent setup sessions (two tabs, or setup then re-setup before enabling) overwrite each other's backup codes; the earlier-shown codes silently fail at login with IncorrectBackupCode and the user has no way to know which set is current.

adjudication.rationale: In `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, backup codes are generated (`crypto.randomBytes...`) and immediately persisted to the user record (`data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...), twoFactorEnabled: false, twoFactorSecret: ... }`) before the user completes the TOTP enable/verification flow. Any subsequent setup call (e.g., retrying setup, re-opening in another tab) will overwrite `users.backupCodes` with a new set, while earlier UI sessions may still display the old codes (EnableTwoFactorModal stores/display `body.backupCodes` from that setup response). This makes previously shown codes silently invalid and can cause `IncorrectBackupCode` at login with no indication of which set is current.
